cards.title: Graph isomorphism parameterized by vertex deletion to planarity
cards.formal: Is there one deterministic algorithm A, a total computable function f:N→N, and an absolute constant c such that, for every h≥0 and every pair of finite simple undirected graphs G₁,G₂ that can each be made planar by deleting at most h vertices, A decides whether G₁≅G₂ in at most f(h)(n+1)^c steps, where n=|V(G₁)|+|V(G₂)|? The input consists of the graphs and h; deletion sets and planar embeddings are not supplied. This uses the usual effective definition of fixed-parameter tractability, including computability of f.
cards.why: Would show that graph isomorphism retains an effective fixed-parameter running-time guarantee under a bounded number of arbitrary vertex additions to a planar graph.
cards.status_note: The broad fixed-parameter-shaped bound follows from the 2022 excluded-minor theorem; its proof statement expressly does not guarantee a computable parameter function. The card asks for the usual effective FPT guarantee. Checked the full published theorem and subsequent searches through 12 September 2026; no result removing this caveat for G_h was identified.

progress.text: The source asks for FPT isomorphism on graphs made planar by deleting at most h vertices.

cards.definitions: For a graph G and X⊆V(G), G−X is the induced graph obtained by deleting X and its incident edges. A graph is planar if it can be drawn in the plane with edges intersecting only at common endpoints. Put a(G)=min{|X|:G−X is planar} and G_h={G:a(G)≤h}. The graphs may be disconnected and have no vertex colors or edge weights. They are encoded by adjacency matrices on numbered vertices; h is a binary integer, and it suffices to consider 0≤h≤n, as larger h can be capped. An isomorphism is a bijection φ:V(G₁)→V(G₂) with {u,v}∈E(G₁) exactly when {φ(u),φ(v)}∈E(G₂). The required output is yes or no, with no error. The algorithm is a uniform deterministic Turing algorithm: one finite program handles all h, and f must be computable by a terminating program on every integer input. The polynomial exponent c is independent of h. The displayed correctness and time guarantees concern promised pairs in G_h; recognition or producing a deletion set is not a separate required output. This parameter is vertex deletion distance to planarity, not Euler genus, edge deletion distance, or an iterated elimination distance.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove or refute the existence of the stated uniform algorithm with a computable parameter bound f and an exponent independent of h. An n^{O(h)} algorithm, a separate polynomial-time algorithm for each fixed h with no uniform computable bound, or a bound f(h)n^c whose f is not shown computable does not establish this effective FPT target.

context_blocks.text: The STOC 2022 theorem gives one algorithm for H-minor-free graphs with time g(H)n^{O(1)}, but explicitly states that g is not guaranteed computable. Its authors note that this falls outside the usual definition of FPT. As a direct class-containment consequence, it also gives a bound depending only on h for G_h: such a graph excludes K_{h+5} as a minor. This consequence retains the same computability caveat.

cards.title: Exact-clique SOS degree lower bounds in G(n,p)
cards.formal: For graphs G sampled from G(n,p), what degree lower bounds hold with high probability for sum-of-squares refutations of the existence of a clique of exactly k vertices, when the edge probability p is allowed to differ from 1/2 and to depend on n? The source particularly asks about small p and suitable clique sizes. Its exact problem keeps the equality ∑ᵢxᵢ=k and all its allowed polynomial consequences. The parameter regime and requested sharpness of the lower bound remain unspecified.
cards.why: Would determine how random-graph density affects the power of semidefinite proof systems when the target cardinality is enforced exactly, rather than through a weaker optimization constraint.
cards.status_note: Read both the exact proof-system definitions and the complete concluding question. Checked the ECCC record, the author’s current papers, and later searches through 12 September 2026. No resolution of this broad density-dependent extension was identified; the source leaves its quantitative target open.

importance.reason: Tests how equality constraints and graph density affect a widely used algorithmic proof system. Existing score retained.

sentences: The input is an ordinary random graph with independent edge probability p.
The proof system tries to refute a clique of a specified exact size using polynomial equations and sums of squares.
The exact size equation must hold under all permitted polynomial multipliers, unlike the weaker expected-size relaxation.
The source proves strong degree lower bounds at p=1/2 and asks for corresponding bounds at other densities, especially sparse ones.
It does not choose the relationship between density and clique size or the required precision of those bounds.

cards.definitions: G(n,p) is the distribution of simple undirected graphs on [n] in which each unordered pair is independently an edge with probability p. Here 0<p<1 and 1≤k≤n is an integer target clique size. No clique is planted in the sampled graph; “planted clique” in the paper’s title refers to the algorithmic motivation. For a fixed G, the polynomial equations over R are xᵢ²−xᵢ=0 for every i, xᵢxⱼ=0 for each nonedge {i,j}, and ∑ᵢxᵢ−k=0. A degree-d SOS refutation is a polynomial identity −1=∑_a q_a F_a+∑_b r_b², where F_a run over these equations’ left sides, the multipliers q_a and r_b have real coefficients, deg(q_a F_a)≤d, and 2deg(r_b)≤d. Proof size and coefficient bit length are not the cost being asked about. Equivalently for a sufficient lower-bound certificate, a degree-d pseudoexpectation is a linear functional L on polynomials of degree at most d with L(1)=1, L(q²)≥0 whenever 2deg(q)≤d, and L(qF_a)=0 whenever deg(qF_a)≤d. In particular, the size equality must hold after multiplication by every admissible q; requiring only L(∑ᵢxᵢ)≥k is the weaker non-exact formulation. Write D(G,k) for the minimum refutation degree and set D=∞ when no refutation exists. A high-probability degree lower bound d(n) means Pr[D(G,k(n))≥d(n)]→1 as n→∞, with G∼G(n,p(n)). To express a nontrivial refutation lower bound, the chosen regime should also have no k(n)-clique with probability tending to one; satisfiable instances admit no refutation for the elementary reason that their equations have a solution.
cards.answer_criterion: After specifying a source-compatible regime for p(n), k(n), the desired lower-bound scale and probability guarantee, prove that every exact-clique SOS refutation has at least that degree with the required probability. A result only for the weaker expected-size inequality, only for p=1/2, or relying on the typical existence of an actual k-clique does not answer the intended extension.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
